conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping care for you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really tired and my legs have been swelling up over the past few weeks. I’ve gained about 7 pounds even though I’ve been taking my old Lasix pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any shortness of breath or trouble lying flat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I don’t have trouble breathing. But I have been feeling kind of off—just weak and not myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you were recently diagnosed with a urinary tract infection and started on an antibiotic called cefpodoxime. How’s that been going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m taking it, but I still feel sluggish. My blood sugar was really high at urgent care—388—and my white blood cell count went up. I’m worried it’s not working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history with kidney transplants and diabetes, we have to be careful. We’ve checked your labs and chest X-ray, and there’s no sign of pneumonia or heart issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. But why the leg swelling? Is my heart or kidneys failing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is stable, and your heart enzymes are normal. We did an ultrasound of your legs to check for blood clots—it came back negative. So it’s likely fluid buildup from your kidneys not responding fully to the diuretic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. Should I take more Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to restart Lasix, but at a different schedule—20 mg every other day. We want to avoid drying you out, especially since your blood pressure is already on the lower side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning look better. Your white count has come down, and your glucose is 220—still high, but improving. The blood culture showed no infection, and CMV is negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the EBV test I heard about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The EBV test was positive for past infection, but not active. So it’s not causing your current symptoms. We think your fatigue and swelling are mostly due to the UTI and fluid retention, possibly worsened by stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have been under a lot of stress… my dad passed away two weeks ago. I haven’t been sleeping or eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry to hear that. Grief can really affect your body, especially with your medical history. We’ll keep supporting you. Your transplant team is involved, and you’re on the right medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your leg swelling has improved, and you’re feeling more alert. We’re going to discharge you today with instructions to continue cefpodoxime for your UTI and take Lasix every other day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I adjust the Lasix if I feel swollen again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—check your weight daily. If you gain more than 2 pounds, call your kidney doctor. They’ll guide any dose changes. Also, keep up with your weekly labs and follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I should keep using my insulin pump the same way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep using your pump as before, check your sugars regularly, and take all your other medications, including prednisone and cyclosporine, to protect your transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your urine culture came back contaminated, so we can’t rely on it. But since your symptoms are improving on cefpodoxime, we’ll continue it as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also monitor your thyroid. Your TSH was a bit high, but we’ll follow up with your regular doctor on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll keep that in mind for my next appointment.
